objectives: Evaluate an integral over an infinite interval.
Evaluate an integral over a closed interval with an infinite discontinuity within the interval.
Use the comparison theorem to determine whether a definite integral is convergent.

body.text: Is the area between the graph of $f(x)=\frac{1}{x}$ and the *x*-axis over the interval $[1,+\infty )$ finite or infinite? If this same region is revolved about the *x*-axis, is the volume finite or infinite? Surprisingly, the area of the region described is infinite, but the volume of the solid obtained by revolving this region about the *x*-axis is finite.

In this section, we define integrals over an infinite interval as well as integrals of functions containing a discontinuity on the interval. Integrals of these types are called improper integrals. We examine several techniques for evaluating improper integrals, all of which involve taking limits.

How should we go about defining an integral of the type ${\displaystyle \int_{a}^{+\infty}f(x)dx}?$ We can integrate ${\displaystyle \int_{a}^{t}f(x)dx}$ for any value of $t,$ so it is reasonable to look at the behavior of this integral as we substitute larger values of $t.$ Figure 3.16 shows that ${\displaystyle \int_{a}^{t}f(x)dx}$ may be interpreted as area for various values of $t.$ In other words, we may define an improper integral as a limit, taken as one of the limits of integration increases or decreases without bound.

Under all three curves is a shaded region bounded by a on the x-axis an t on the x-axis. The region in the first curve is small, and progressively gets wider under the second and third graph as t moves further to the right away from a on the x-axis.
body.caption: **Figure 3.16** To integrate a function over an infinite interval, we consider the limit of the integral as the upper limit increases without bound.

body.text: In our first example, we return to the question we posed at the start of this section: Is the area between the graph of $f(x)=\frac{1}{x}$ and the $x$-axis over the interval $[1,+\infty )$ finite or infinite?

problem.text: Determine whether the area between the graph of $f(x)=\frac{1}{x}$ and the *x*-axis over the interval $[1,+\infty )$ is finite or infinite.

body.text: We first do a quick sketch of the region in question, as shown in the following graph.

body.alt: This figure is the graph of the function y = 1/x. It is a decreasing function with a vertical asymptote at the y-axis. In the first quadrant there is a shaded region under the curve bounded by x = 1 and x = 4.
body.caption: **Figure 3.17** We can find the area between the curve $f(x)=1/x$ and the *x*-axis on an infinite interval.

body.text: We can see that the area of this region is given by $A={\displaystyle \int_{1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{x}dx}.$ Then we have

body.tex: \begin{array}{ccccc}A & ={\displaystyle \int_{1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{x}dx} & & & \\ & =\lim_{t\to +\infty}{\displaystyle \int_{1}^{t}\frac{1}{x}dx} & & & \text{Rewrite the improper integral as a limit.} \\ & =\lim_{t\to +\infty}\ln |x||{}_{\begin{array}{c} \\ 1\end{array}}^{\begin{array}{c}t \\ \end{array}} & & & \text{Find the antiderivative.} \\ & =\lim_{t\to +\infty}(\ln |t|-\ln \,1) & & & \text{Evaluate the antiderivative.} \\ & =+\infty . & & & \text{Evaluate the limit.}\end{array}

body.text: Since the improper integral diverges to $+\infty ,$ the area of the region is infinite.

problem.text: Find the volume of the solid obtained by revolving the region bounded by the graph of $f(x)=\frac{1}{x}$ and the *x*-axis over the interval $[1,+\infty )$ about the $x$-axis.

body.text: The solid is shown in Figure 3.18. Using the disk method, we see that the volume *V* is

body.alt: This figure is the graph of the function y = 1/x. It is a decreasing function with a vertical asymptote at the y-axis. The graph shows a solid that has been generated by rotating the curve in the first quadrant around the x-axis.
body.caption: **Figure 3.18** The solid of revolution can be generated by rotating an infinite area about the *x*-axis.

body.tex: \begin{array}{ccccc}V & =\pi {\displaystyle \int_{1}^{+\infty}\frac{1}{x^{2}}dx} & & & \\ & =\pi \lim_{t\to +\infty}{\displaystyle \int_{1}^{t}\frac{1}{x^{2}}dx} & & & \text{Rewrite as a limit.} \\ & =\pi \lim_{t\to +\infty}-\frac{1}{x}|{}_{\begin{array}{c} \\ 1\end{array}}^{\begin{array}{c}t \\ \end{array}} & & & \text{Find the antiderivative.} \\ & =\pi \lim_{t\to +\infty}\left(-\,\frac{1}{t}+1\right) & & & \text{Evaluate the antiderivative.} \\ & =\pi . & & & \end{array}

body.text: The improper integral converges to $\pi .$ Therefore, the volume of the solid of revolution is $\pi .$

In conclusion, although the area of the region between the *x*-axis and the graph of $f(x)=1/x$ over the interval $[1,+\infty )$ is infinite, the volume of the solid generated by revolving this region about the *x*-axis is finite. The solid generated is known as **Gabriel’s Horn**.

problem.text: In the chapter opener, we stated the following problem: Suppose that at a busy intersection, **traffic accidents** occur at an average rate of one every three months. After residents complained, changes were made to the traffic lights at the intersection. It has now been ten months since the changes were made and there have been no accidents. Were the changes effective or is the 10-month interval without an accident a result of chance?

problem.text: Evaluate ${\displaystyle \int_{-\infty}^{0}\frac{1}{x^{2}+4}dx}.$ State whether the improper integral converges or diverges.

body.text: Begin by rewriting ${\displaystyle \int_{-\infty}^{0}\frac{1}{x^{2}+4}dx}$ as a limit using (see above) from the definition. Thus,

body.tex: \begin{array}{ccccc}{\displaystyle \int_{-\infty}^{0}\frac{1}{x^{2}+4}dx} & =\lim_{x\to -\infty}{\displaystyle \int_{t}^{0}\frac{1}{x^{2}+4}dx} & & & \text{Rewrite as a limit.} \\ & =\lim_{t\to -\infty}\frac{1}{2}\tan^{-1}\frac{x}{2}|{}_{\begin{array}{c} \\ t\end{array}}^{\begin{array}{c}0 \\ \end{array}} & & & \text{Find the antiderivative.} \\ & =\frac{1}{2}\lim_{t\to -\infty}(\tan^{-1}0-\tan^{-1}\frac{t}{2}) & & & \text{Evaluate the antiderivative.} \\ & =\frac{\pi}{4}. & & & \text{Evaluate the limit and simplify.}\end{array}

reading.title: Evaluating an Improper Integral over an Infinite Interval

problem.text: Evaluate ${\displaystyle \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty}xe^{x}dx}.$ State whether the improper integral converges or diverges.

body.text: Start by splitting up the integral:

If either ${\displaystyle \int_{-\infty}^{0}xe^{x}dx}$ or ${\displaystyle \int_{0}^{+\infty}xe^{x}dx}$ diverges, then ${\displaystyle \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty}xe^{x}dx}$ diverges. Compute each integral separately. For the first integral,

body.tex: \begin{array}{ccccc}{\displaystyle \int_{-\infty}^{0}xe^{x}dx} & =\lim_{t\to -\infty}{\displaystyle \int_{t}^{0}xe^{x}dx} & & & \text{Rewrite as a limit.} \\ & =\lim_{t\to -\infty}(xe^{x}-e^{x})|{}_{\begin{array}{c} \\ t\end{array}}^{\begin{array}{c}0 \\ \end{array}} & & & \begin{array}{c}\text{Use integration by parts to find the} \\ \text{antiderivative. (Here}\,u=x\,\text{and}\,dv=e^{x}\mathrm{dx}.)\end{array} \\ & =\lim_{t\to -\infty}(-1-te^{t}+e^{t}) & & & \text{Evaluate the antiderivative.} \\ & =-1. & & & \begin{array}{c}\text{Evaluate the limit.}\,\text{Note:}\,\lim_{t\to -\infty}te^{t}\,\text{is} \\ \text{indeterminate of the form}\,0\cdot \infty .\,\text{Thus,} \\ \lim_{t\to -\infty}te^{t}=\lim_{t\to -\infty}\frac{t}{e^{-t}}=\lim_{t\to -\infty}\frac{-1}{e^{-t}}=\lim_{t\to -\infty}-e^{t}=0\,\text{by} \\ \text{L’Hôpital’s Rule.}\end{array}\end{array}

body.text: The first improper integral converges. For the second integral,

body.tex: \begin{array}{ccccc}{\displaystyle \int_{0}^{+\infty}xe^{x}dx} & =\lim_{t\to +\infty}{\displaystyle \int_{0}^{t}xe^{x}dx} & & & \text{Rewrite as a limit.} \\ & =\lim_{t\to +\infty}(xe^{x}-e^{x})|{}_{\begin{array}{c} \\ 0\end{array}}^{\begin{array}{c}t \\ \end{array}} & & & \text{Find the antiderivative.} \\ & =\lim_{t\to +\infty}(te^{t}-e^{t}+1) & & & \text{Evaluate the antiderivative.} \\ & =\lim_{t\to +\infty}((t-1)e^{t}+1) & & & \text{Rewrite.}\,(te^{t}-e^{t}\,\text{is indeterminate.)} \\ & =+\infty . & & & \text{Evaluate the limit.}\end{array}

body.text: Thus, ${\displaystyle \int_{0}^{+\infty}xe^{x}dx}$ diverges. Since this integral diverges, ${\displaystyle \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty}xe^{x}dx}$ diverges as well.

body.text: Now let’s examine integrals of functions containing an infinite discontinuity in the interval over which the integration occurs. Consider an integral of the form ${\displaystyle \int_{a}^{b}f(x)dx,}$ where $f(x)$ is continuous over $[a,b)$ and discontinuous at $b.$ Since the function $f(x)$ is continuous over $[a,t]$ for all values of $t$ satisfying $a<t<b,$ the integral ${\displaystyle \int_{a}^{t}f(x)dx}$ is defined for all such values of $t.$ Thus, it makes sense to consider the values of ${\displaystyle \int_{a}^{t}f(x)dx}$ as $t$ approaches $b$ for $a<t<b.$ That is, we define ${\displaystyle \int_{a}^{b}f(x)dx=\lim_{t\to b^{-}}{\displaystyle \int_{a}^{t}f(x)dx}},$ provided this limit exists. Figure 3.20 illustrates ${\displaystyle \int_{a}^{t}f(x)dx}$ as areas of regions for values of $t$ approaching $b.$

body.alt: This figure has three graphs. All the graphs have the same curve, which is f(x). The curve is non-negative, only in the first quadrant, and increasing. Under all three curves is a shaded region bounded by a on the x-axis an t on the x-axis. There is also a vertical asymptote at x = b. The region in the first curve is small, and progressively gets wider under the second and third graph as t gets further from a, and closer to b on the x-axis.
body.caption: **Figure 3.20** As *t* approaches *b* from the left, the value of the area from *a* to *t* approaches the area from *a* to *b*.

body.text: We use a similar approach to define ${\displaystyle \int_{a}^{b}f(x)dx,}$ where $f(x)$ is continuous over $(a,b]$ and discontinuous at $a.$ We now proceed with a formal definition.

problem.text: Evaluate ${\displaystyle \int_{0}^{4}\frac{1}{\sqrt{4-x}}dx},$ if possible. State whether the integral converges or diverges.

body.text: The function $f(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{4-x}}$ is continuous over $[0,4)$ and discontinuous at 4. Using (see above) from the definition, rewrite ${\displaystyle \int_{0}^{4}\frac{1}{\sqrt{4-x}}dx}$ as a limit:

body.tex: \begin{array}{ccccc}{\displaystyle \int_{0}^{4}\frac{1}{\sqrt{4-x}}dx} & =\lim_{t\to 4^{-}}{\displaystyle \int_{0}^{t}\frac{1}{\sqrt{4-x}}dx} & & & \text{Rewrite as a limit.} \\ & =\lim_{t\to 4^{-}}(-2\sqrt{4-x})|{}_{\begin{array}{c} \\ 0\end{array}}^{\begin{array}{c}t \\ \end{array}} & & & \text{Find the antiderivative.} \\ & =\lim_{t\to 4^{-}}(-2\sqrt{4-t}+4) & & & \text{Evaluate the antiderivative.} \\ & =4. & & & \text{Evaluate the limit.}\end{array}

problem.text: Evaluate ${\displaystyle \int_{0}^{2}x\,\ln \,x\,dx}.$ State whether the integral converges or diverges.

body.text: Since $f(x)=x\,\ln \,x$ is continuous over $(0,2]$ and is discontinuous at zero, we can rewrite the integral in limit form using (see above):

body.tex: \begin{array}{ccccc}{\displaystyle \int_{0}^{2}x\,\ln \,x\,dx} & =\lim_{t\to 0^{+}}{\displaystyle \int_{t}^{2}x\,\ln \,x\,dx} & & & \text{Rewrite as a limit.} \\ & =\lim_{t\to 0^{+}}\left(\frac{1}{2}x^{2}\ln \,x-\frac{1}{4}x^{2}\right)|{}_{\begin{array}{c} \\ t\end{array}}^{\begin{array}{c}2 \\ \end{array}} & & & \begin{array}{c}\text{Evaluate}\,{\displaystyle \int}^{\text{​}}x\,\ln \,x\,dx\,\text{using integration by parts} \\ \text{with}\,u=\ln \,x\,\text{and}\,dv=x\mathrm{dx}.\end{array} \\ & =\lim_{t\to 0^{+}}\left(2\,\ln \,2-1-\frac{1}{2}t^{2}\ln \,t+\frac{1}{4}t^{2}\right). & & & \text{Evaluate the antiderivative.} \\ & =2\,\ln \,2-1. & & & \begin{array}{c}\text{Evaluate the limit.}\,\lim_{t\to 0^{+}}t^{2}\ln \,t\,\text{is indeterminate.} \\ \text{To evaluate it, rewrite as a quotient and apply} \\ \text{L’Hôpital’s rule.}\end{array}\end{array}

It is not always easy or even possible to evaluate an improper integral directly; however, by comparing it with another carefully chosen integral, it may be possible to determine its convergence or divergence. To see this, consider two continuous functions $f(x)$ and $g(x)$ satisfying $0\le f(x)\le g(x)$ for $x\ge a$ (Figure 3.21). In this case, we may view integrals of these functions over intervals of the form $[a,t]$ as areas, so we have the relationship

It has a sharper bend in the curve compared to g(x). The graph of g(x) is a decreasing, non-negative function with a horizontal asymptote at the x-axis.
body.caption: **Figure 3.21** If $0\le f(x)\le g(x)$ for $x\ge a,$ then for $t\ge a,$ ${\displaystyle \int_{a}^{t}f(x)dx\le {\displaystyle \int_{a}^{t}g(x)dx}}.$

body.text: ${\displaystyle \int_{a}^{+\infty}g(x)dx=\lim_{t\to +\infty}{\displaystyle \int_{a}^{t}g(x)dx=+\infty}}$ as well. That is, if the area of the region between the graph of $f(x)$ and the *x*-axis over $[a,+\infty )$ is infinite, then the area of the region between the graph of $g(x)$ and the *x*-axis over $[a,+\infty )$ is infinite too.

${\displaystyle \int_{a}^{+\infty}f(x)dx=\lim_{t\to +\infty}{\displaystyle \int_{a}^{t}f(x)dx}}$ must converge to some value less than or equal to $L,$ since ${\displaystyle \int_{a}^{t}f(x)dx}$ increases as $t$ increases and ${\displaystyle \int_{a}^{t}f(x)dx\le L}$ for all $t\ge a.$

If the area of the region between the graph of $g(x)$ and the *x*-axis over $[a,+\infty )$ is finite, then the area of the region between the graph of $f(x)$ and the *x*-axis over $[a,+\infty )$ is also finite.
These conclusions are summarized in the following theorem.
Let $f(x)$ and $g(x)$ be continuous over $[a,+\infty ).$ Assume that $0\le f(x)\le g(x)$ for $x\ge a.$

items: If ${\displaystyle \int_{a}^{+\infty}g(x)dx=\lim_{t\to +\infty}{\displaystyle \int_{a}^{t}g(x)dx=L,}}$ where $L$ is a real number, then ${\displaystyle \int_{a}^{+\infty}f(x)dx=\lim_{t\to +\infty}{\displaystyle \int_{a}^{t}f(x)dx=M}}$ for some real number $M\le L.$

body.text: For $p<1,$ $1/x\le 1/(x^{p})$ over $[1,+\infty ).$ In Example 3.47, we showed that ${\displaystyle \int_{1}^{+\infty}\frac{1}{x}dx=+\infty}.$ Therefore, ${\displaystyle \int_{1}^{+\infty}\frac{1}{x^{p}}dx}$ diverges for all $p<1.$

prompt.text: Show that $f(x)=\{\begin{array}{c}0\,\text{if}\,x<0 \\ 7e^{-7x}\text{if}\,x\ge 0\end{array}$ is a probability density function.

instructions.text: A non-negative function is a **probability density function** if it satisfies the following definition: ${\displaystyle \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f(t)dt=1}.$ The probability that a random variable *x* lies between *a* and *b* is given by $P(a\le x\le b)={\displaystyle \int_{a}^{b}f(t)dt}.$
